speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is strong overall and has made significant progress toward our, our goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has cooled from its formerly overheated state and remains solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moved much closer to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re committed to maintaining our economy’s strength by supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To that end, today, the Federal Open Market Committee decided to take another step in reducing the degree of policy restraint by lowering our policy interest rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also decided to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a—at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at an annual rate of 2.8 percent in the third quarter, about the same pace as in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth of consumer spending has remained resilient, and investment in equipment and intangibles has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, improving supply conditions have supported the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, Committee participants generally expect GDP growth to remain solid, with a median projection of about 2 percent over the next few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions remain solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains have slowed from earlier in the year, averaging 173,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate is higher than it was a year ago, but, at 4.2 percent in November, it has remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a broad set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are now less tight than in 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection for the unemployment rate in the SEP is 4.2 percent at the end of this year and 4.3 percent over the next few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly over the past two years but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.5 percent over the 12 months ending in November, and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 2.4 percent this year and 2.5 percent next year, somewhat higher than projected in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thereafter, the median projection falls to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals as being roughly in balance, and we are attentive to the risks on both sides of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point, to 4¼-4½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been moving policy toward a more neutral setting in order to maintain the strength of the economy and the labor market while establishing further progress in—sorry, enabling further progress on—inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With today’s action, we have lowered our policy rate by a full percentage point from its peak, and our policy stance is now significantly less restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can therefore be more cautious as we consider further adjustments to our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too fast or too much could hinder progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too slowly or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not on any preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.9 percent at the end of next year and 3.4 percent at the end of 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These median projections are somewhat higher than in September, consistent with the firmer inflation projection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These projections, however, are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, monetary policy will adjust in order to best promote our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains strong and inflation does not continue to move sustainably toward 2 percent, we can dial back policy restraint more slowly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we can ease policy more quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On a technical note: We lowered the offering rate on our overnight reverse repo facility to align it with the bottom of the target range for the federal funds rate—its typical configuration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Technical adjustments of this kind have no bearing on the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, so let, let me start by saying why we—why we cut today and then—and then move to 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say today was a—was a closer call, but we decided it was the right call because we thought it was the best decision to foster achievement of both of our goals, maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the risks as two-sided: moving too slowly and needlessly undermine economic activity and the labor market, or move too quickly and needlessly undermine our progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re trying to steer between those two risks, and, on balance, we decided to go ahead with a further cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I’ll give you some details on why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Downside risks to the labor market do appear to have diminished, but the labor market is now looser than pre-pandemic, and it’s clearly still cooling further, so far in, in a gradual and orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think we need further cooling in the labor market to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation is now well below the level or certainly below the level that would hold unemployment constant, the job-finding rate is low and declining, and other measures—such as surveys of workers and businesses, quits, things like that—broadly show a, a much cooler labor market than there was, than we had in 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still quite gradually cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we keep an eye on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation, we see that story as still broadly on track, and, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’ve made a great deal of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Twelve-month core inflation, as I mentioned, through November is estimated at 2.8 percent, down from a high of 5.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Twelve—but 12-month inflation has actually been moving sideways, as we are “lapping” very low readings of late last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Housing services inflation actually is steadily coming down now, albeit at a slower pace than we might like, but it has now come down substantially and it is making progress, slower than hoped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we, we’ve had recent high readings from nonmarket services and some bumpiness for goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll just say, we, we—so remember that we couple this decision today with the “extent and timing” language in the postmeeting statement that signals that we are at or near a point at which it will be appropriate to slow the pace of further adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You ask about 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think that the lower—the slower pace of cuts for next year really reflects both the higher inflation readings we’ve had this year and the expectation that inflation will be higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw in the SEP that risks and, and uncertainty around inflation we see as higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, we, we see ourselves as, as still on track to continue to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the actual cuts that we make next year will not be because of anything we wrote down today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re going to react to data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s just the general sense of what the Committee thinks is likely to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re—to, to cut further after this point, I, I would say it this way: We’ve reduced our policy rate now by 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re significantly closer to neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At 4.3 percent and “change,” we believe policy is still meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as for additional cuts, we’re going to be looking for further progress on inflation as well as continued strength in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as long as the economy and the labor market are solid, we can be cautious about—as we consider further cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And all of that is reflected—to your question—in the December SEP, which shows a median forecast of down [to] two cuts next year, compared to four in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I’d say—I’d, I’d point to five or six things, and, and I’d start—let me start by saying that we think the economy’s in a really good place, and we think policy’s in a really good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s remember that the economy’s growing 2½ percent this year, that inflation has come down by 50 percent to, to—from 5.6 percent to 2.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Headline inflation is 2.5 percent on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re actually in a really good starting place here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, the economy grew faster in the second half of 2024, so far, than we had expected and is expected to be above what our expectations in September next year as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Unemployment is lower, and, you know, in the SEP, you’ll see that participants think that the—that the downside risks are less and uncertainty is less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is higher, as we talked about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation’s higher this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also higher in the forecast next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d also point out that we’re, we’re closer to the neutral rate, which is another reason to be cautious about, about further moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And—but then getting to your—to your point, there’s also, there’s uncertainty—uncertainty around inflation, I pointed out, is actually higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also—it’s also, in the case of some people, some people—the way I’d say it is this: Some people did take a very preliminary step and start to incorporate highly conditional estimates of economic effects of policies into their forecast at this meeting and said so in the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some people said they didn’t do so, and some people didn’t, didn’t say whether they did or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have people making a bunch of different approaches to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But some did identify policy uncertainty as one of the reasons for their, their writing down more uncertainty around inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the point of that uncertainty is, it’s kind of commonsense thinking that when the path is uncertain you go a little bit slower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not unlike driving on a foggy night or walking into a dark room full of furniture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You just slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that may have affected some of the people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as, as I said, there’s a range of—range of approaches on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Actually, that’s not the only thing that’s happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What’s happened is that our forecast for inflation for this year, I think, are five-tenths higher than they were in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you’ve got—you had two months of higher inflation, September and October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, November is, is back on track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, once again we’ve, you know, we’ve had a year-end projection for inflation and it’s kind of fallen apart as we’ve approached the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that is certainly a large factor in people’s thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can tell you that might be the single biggest factor is inflation has once again underperformed relative to expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still, you know, going to be between 2½ and 3 [percent].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s way below where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we really want to see progress on inflation, to, to, you know, as I mentioned, as we think about further cuts, we’re going to be looking for progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have been moving sideways on 12-month inflation as the 12-month window moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s in part because inflation was very, very low measured in, in the 4th quarter of 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, as we go forward, we’re going to want to be seeing further progress on bringing inflation down and keeping a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I do think that the 2018, the September 2018 Tealbook alternative simulations are a good place to start.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I happened to have brought them here with me today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m sure you have them too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re, they’re a good starting point, and, and I would just say, you know, it’s six-years-old analysis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But nonetheless, this is still, I think, I think the right, the right questions to ask.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, there, there were two simulations: one was—one was “seeing through,” one was not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I point you to, you’ll— there’s some language in the—in the “see-through” paragraph.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It says, you know, it considers situations in which it might be appropriate to “see through” inflation and then, and then names some conditions that in, in which it might not be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In any case, this is not a question that’s in front of us right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we won’t face that question—we don’t know when we’ll face that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What the Committee’s doing now is, is discussing pathways and understanding, again, the ways in which tariff-driven inflation can affect—tariffs can affect inflation and the economy, and, and how to think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we’re, we’re—we’ve done a bit of, good bit of work, all of us have, each of us has, and, you know, it puts us in position, when we finally do see what the, what the actual policies are, to be, to make, you know, a more, more careful, thoughtful assessment of what might be the appropriate policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the, the main thing is—and this is also a point in these alternative simulations—is that there’re just many, many factors that go into what, what—how much tariffs will, will even go into consumer inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, so, we just—we just don’t know, really, very much at all about the actual policies, so it’s very premature to try to make any kind of conclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what’ll be tariffed, from what countries, for how long, and what size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know whether there’ll be, you know, retaliatory tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what the, you know, the transmission of any of that will be into consumer prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To your—to your point as well, I don’t—I wouldn’t say that we know whether the last episode is or is not a good model for what happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You pointed out we’ve just been through a period of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve just gotten through that period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a difference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was also quite a bit of diversion of trade away from China to other countries, since that, that may—that may have affects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just think we, we need to take our time, not rush, and make a very careful assessment, but only when we’ve actually seen what the policies are and how they’re implemented.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re just—we’re just not at that stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re at the stage of doing what other forecasters are doing—which is kind of thinking about these questions, but not, not trying to get to definitive answers for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let me—let me find these numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have—we have inflation coming down, core inflation coming down to 2½ [percent] next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’d be—that’d be significant progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see a slower path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that does take on board that we want to see real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we, we, you know, we’d be seeing meaningful progress to get inflation down to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That wouldn’t be all the way to 2 percent, but that would be, it would be, you know, better than this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This year, [it] will be 2.8 or 2.9.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That would be meaningful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we also have to think about the, the, you know, the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And while we, we have the labor market forecast as being in good shape, we are also mindful that it is still out there very gradually cooling, so far in an orderly, gradual way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s also something we need to keep our eye on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s not the—that’s not any decision that we’ve made at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let me explain “extent and timing.” So the, the sense of that wording is to make clear that if the economy does evolve about as anticipated, we’re at a point at which it would be appropriate to slow the pace of rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So “extent,” that just relates to how, how much further we can reduce our policy rate consistent with getting to a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Clearly, that distance has shrunk by 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s significantly smaller.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s the “extent” question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we’re going to be looking for further progress on inflation, as well as a strong labor market, to make those cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: “Timing” just suggests, again, that we’re at a place where we, we, assuming the economy develops as expected, we’re at or near a level that will make it appropriate to slow the pace of adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that’s what we mean by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not trying to make decisions about the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we are, we’re trying to make sensible policy as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I just would emphasize the uncertainty, which is, it’s just—it’s just a function of the fact that, that we expect significant policy changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s nothing really unusual about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we need to, we need to see what they are and see what the effects they will have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll, we’ll have a much clearer picture, I think, you know, when that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the, the risks that you—sorry, the rates that you talked about are, are really longer-run rates, and they’re affected, they are affected to some extent by Fed policy, but they’re also affected by many other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And longer rates have actually gone up quite a bit since September, as, as you well know, and those are the things that drive, for example, mortgage rates more than short-term rates do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at that, but we look at all financial conditions, and then we look at what’s happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we see happening in the economy, again, is, you know, most forecasters have been calling for a slowdown in growth for a very long time, and it keeps not happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have—we’re now well into another year of growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It looks like it might be 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Third and—second and third quarters were right about at the same level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the U.S. economy is just performing very, very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Substantially better than our global peer group.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I—there’s no reason to think a downturn is, is any more likely than it—than it usually is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, the outlook is pretty bright for our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to stay on task, though, and continue to have restrictive policies so that we can get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also going to be looking out for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to keep the labor market pretty close to where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re pretty close to estimates of the, the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation is, is a little below the, the level that would keep it there but, nonetheless, close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s what our policy’s trying to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So confidence was our test for raising rates, and, you know, we’ve made—look, look at the broader suite: We’ve made just a great deal of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, you know, we’re well into the 2’s in, in core inflation and around 2½ [percent]—or even lower than that, we have been—for headline inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I would say I’m confident that inflation has come down a great deal, and I, I’m confident in the story about why it’s come down and why that portends well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’ll—and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You, again, you do see with housing services inflation, which is one that we’ve really worried, worried about, it really has come down now quite steadily, at a slower pace than we thought, you know, two years ago, but it’s nonetheless steadily coming down as, as market rents, you know, market rents start to equilibrate better with, you know, new leases that turn over.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not, not new tenants, but new leases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Market rents is new leases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that’s happening; that process is ongoing pretty much as we expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Goods inflation, which is another big piece of it, has returned right to the range where it was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Just for some months this year it kind of moved up in a bumpy way because of used cars and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we think, overall, that should generally be in the range it was in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then that leaves nonhousing services, and market-based nonhousing services are in, in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s nonmarket services, and those are—those are services that are imputed rather than measured directly, and they, they don’t, we, we think they don’t really tell us much about the, you know, about tightness in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They don’t really reflect that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, a good example is financial services, which is really done off of asset prices, and that just—so that, that’s how that inflation works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the overall picture, the story of why inflation should be coming down, is still intact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In particular, the labor market—look at the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it is cooler by so many measures now—modestly cooler than it was in 2019, a year when inflation was well under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not a source of inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not to say there aren’t regional and, and, you know, particular professions where labor is tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, you’re not getting inflationary impulses of any significance from the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The story is still just, we’re unwinding from these large shocks that the economy got in 2021 and ’22 in, for example, housing services, and now also in, in insurance, in particular, where costs went up, and those are now being reflected later in housing insurance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s real inflation, but it doesn’t portend persistently high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we and most other forecasters still feel that we’re on track to, you know, to get down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It might take another year or two from here, but I, I’m confident that that’s the path we’re on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, our policy will do everything it can to assure that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The, the unemployment rate has now—is now the same as it was in July: 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s moved up and down, but it’s now the same as July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And job creation is, is lower than it has been, but it’s been—it’s been steady—it’s not—it’s not declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been steady at a level which, as I pointed out a couple times, is actually below the level that would hold the unemployment rate constant, but it’s not so far below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you might—you might—if, if we have the, the breakeven level right, and if jobs continue—job creation continues at that level in the establishment survey, then you would get a tenth maybe every other month kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So gradually declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we don’t have that kind of precision in this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, but you’re right, though, and I, I read out some of the reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we do think the labor market is still cooling by many measures, and we’re watching that closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it’s not cooling in a—in a quick or in a way that really raises concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, you know, you pointed out participants in the FOMC really thought that the risks and uncertainty had improved relative to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s because of, because things have just gotten a little bit better, it doesn’t—the unemployment rate flat and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, you know, we’re watching it closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I—what I said is, we don’t think we need further softening to get to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what I’m saying, not that it’s not welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t need it, we don’t think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If, if you had a situation where inflation’s moving around by a tenth every few months, that’s, you know, we’d have to weigh that against the fact that inflation has in recent months been moving sideways in the 12-month window.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’ve got to weigh them both, at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, for a while there we were only really focused mainly, mainly focused on, on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve now gotten to a place where, where the risks of the two are what we think are broadly, roughly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not—we’re not renaming the phase—yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we may get around to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, no, I, I would say we, we are, though, in, in a new phase in the process, as I said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and that’s just because we’ve reduced—we’ve reduced our policy rate by 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re significantly closer to neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We still think where we are is meaningfully, meaningfully restrictive, and I think from this point forward, you know, it’s appropriate to move cautiously and look for progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve, you know, we’ve done a lot to support economic activity by cutting 100 basis points, and that’s a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think it would—I support the decision, and, and I think it was the right decision to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think from now we are in a place where the risks really are in balance, and we need to see progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s how we’re thinking about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it is kind of a new thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We moved pretty quickly to get to here, and I think going forward, obviously, we’re going to be moving slower, which is consistent with, with the SEP. STEVE LIESMAN.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wonder if I could follow up and ask you how much you or the Committee are looking through some of the high numbers we’ve had in the recent inflation numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For example, cars being up maybe because of the hurricanes, eggs because of the avian flu, that, that kind of stuff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and then looking forward, perhaps, to housing inflation coming down, as it did in the recent report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve got, we have a very low month, potentially, in November.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s estimated by many to be in the mid-teens for core PCE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that could be idiosyncratically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We try to look—we try to look at not just a couple or three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We shouldn’t have—our, our position shouldn’t change based on two or three months of good or bad data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have a long string now of inflation coming down gradually over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, 12-month, I think it’s 12-month headline’s 2½; 12-month core is 2.8.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s way better than we were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We still have some work to do, though, is how we’re looking at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we need policy to remain restrictive to, to get—to get that work done, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we do look carefully at financial conditions, of course; that’s part of what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we, we really look carefully at is the performance of our—of our goal variables and, and how are we affecting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we’ve seen over the course of—just take the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’ve seen inflation—well, over the last couple of years—come down a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen the labor market cool off quite a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That suggests that our policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve, we can also look more directly at, at the parts of the economy that are affected by—that, that are interest sensitive, like particularly housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Housing activity is, is very low, and that’s partly, significantly because of our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we think our policy is working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s transmitting, and it’s having the effects on our goal variables that we would want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, a lot of things move financial conditions around, as you know, and we don’t really control those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’d say we, we see the effects we’re hoping to see on, on the goal variables and, and the places where we’d expect to see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we, we’re not allowed to own Bitcoin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Federal Reserve Act says what we can own, and we’re, we’re not looking for a, a law change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the kind of thing for Congress to consider, but we are not looking for a law change at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s pretty clear we’ve avoided a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think growth this year has, has been solid, it really has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: PDFP, private domestic final purchases, which, which we think is the best indicator of private demand, is looking to come in around 3 percent [real growth] this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is a really good number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, the U.S. economy has just been remarkable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s—when we, in these international meetings that I attend, this has been the story, is that how well the U.S. is doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you look around the world, there’s just a lot of slow growth and continued struggles with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I feel—I feel very good about where the economy is and the performance of the economy, and we want to keep that going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think so, no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, overall, if you look at it, prime-age participation is still very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What, what’s going on in the labor market is that the hiring rate is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are not losing their jobs in large numbers, unusually large numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you are looking for a job, though, the hiring rate is low, and that’s a signal of, of lower demand, and it has come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look for signs like that, and that, that’s clearly a sign of softening, further softening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I didn’t mention it earlier, but I, I think you can see a, an ongoing gradual softening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, not something we need to see to get 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that’s part of the reason that explains why we moved ahead today with, with our, with the action, with, with an additional cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, but you take a step back, the level of unemployment is very low—again, participation is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are at a healthy and, and ever more sustainable level—wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so the labor market—this is a good, a good labor market, and, you know, we want to keep it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we can’t know that with any tremendous certainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I will say that we think that, that our policy balances the risks—we think the risks are roughly in balance as between the two mandates, and we think the labor market is, is in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And when I say it’s softening or cooling, it’s very gradual process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, job creations are, are meaningfully positive; wages are, you know, if anything, a little, still a bit above what would be sustainable if productivity were to revert to its longer-run trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you, if you take into account the high productivity readings we’ve had, then wages are already at a sustainable level relative to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, again, I, I don’t want to overstate the downside in the labor market, because the downsides clearly appear to have diminished.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, it’s, it’s one of our mandate goals, and, you know, we pay close attention to it, and it’s, it’s worth noting that it is still gradually cooling—gradually and in an orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, that’s, that’s how I would characterize it, and that’s why we’re paying careful attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it, it breaks down into a long answer, if you want, but it just has been a little bit more stubborn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if you go back two or three years, many people were saying that to get this far down we would’ve had to have a, had a deep recession and, you know, high unemployment by now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, that has not been the case, so, you know, the, the path down has actually been much better than many predicted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’ve managed to, to have the unemployment rate remain essentially at its longer-run natural rate, while inflation has come down from—you know, core PCE inflation has come down from 5.6 percent to 2.8 percent on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s a pretty good outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One reason is that, that—just a technical issue around the way we calculate housing services, and that, that process has been slower than—market rents have, are showing up more slowly in that measure than we might have thought three, two, two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think there are other, other parts of the story, but, you know, the, the—what, what I think people are feeling right now is the effect of high prices, not high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we understand very well that prices went up by a great deal, and people really feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s prices of food and transportation and heating your home and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s tremendous pain in, in that burst of inflation that was very global.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This was everywhere in all the advanced economies at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So now we have—inflation itself is way down, but people are still feeling high prices, and that is—that is really what people are feeling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The best we can do for them—and that’s who we work for—is to get inflation back down to its target and keep it there so that people are earning, you know, big, real wage increases so that their, their wages are going up, their, their compensation is going up faster than inflation year upon year upon year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what will restore people’s good feeling about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what it will take, and that’s what we’re aiming for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I feel—I feel very good about where the economy is, and, honestly, I’m very optimistic about, about the economy, and it’s—we’re, we’re in a really good place; our policy’s in a really good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I expect another good year next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll say a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: First of all, when we, when we write—the thing we write down in the Summary of Economic Projections is the longer-run neutral rate, which is the neutral rate at a time when supply and demand are in balance, the full economy’s in balance, and no shocks are hitting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is not where we are right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when we’re making monetary policy at the Fed, that’s not the question we’re asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can’t do a straight read between those longer-run numbers that we write down and what we think the appropriate policy should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, basically, at any given time, various shocks are hitting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so what we’re doing in, in real time is we’re looking at our policy stance, and we’re looking at the way it’s hitting the economy, and, particularly, we look at the effects it’s having as we try to move the economy toward maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the answer can be that there are things that affect the economy that are—that are lasting but not permanent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the, the ones that are permanent are the ones that would be in r*.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The ones that are, could be lasting, but, but nonetheless go away over time, they could actually affect what, what’s sort of technically the appropriate neutral stance in near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re looking at that, and, you know, we don’t—we don’t know exactly where it is, but as I like to say, we know it by its works, and I think what, what we know for sure is that we’re 100 basis points closer to it right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are many estimates of where that might be, and we know we’re a lot closer to it, and I think we’re in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think from here it’s a new phase, and we’re going to be, you know, cautious about, about further cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I mean, honestly, we—you know, there are countless models of what—of what a neutral rate might be at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There, there are empirical models, there are theoretical models, there are things that combine them, and they have as many different answers as you’d like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there is no real certainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, it’s, it’s actually a good thing to know that we don’t know exactly where it is, so you’re not—you’re not tempted to think, “Oh, I think this model or this estimate is right.” You, you just have to be open to, you know, the empirical data that are coming in and also how it’s affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not made any easier by the fact that, you know, that our policy works with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, that is the job we have, and so we’re, we’re— I think we need— it’s appropriate for us—for us now to proceed cautiously, now that we’re 100 basis points closer to, to neutral, and we’ll do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Meanwhile, the economy seems to be in, in good shape, and these cuts will certainly help to support economic activity and the labor market while we can still make progress on inflation, because policy is still meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and as, as I imagine you know, the, you know, the goal overall is headline inflation, because that’s what people experience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People don’t experience core inflation; they experience inflation, and that includes food and energy costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the overall goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, as we know, headline inflation contains energy and food, and those prices can fluctuate for reasons that are not related to tightness in the economy and therefore are not really good predictors of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it turns out that core inflation is, is a better predictor of overall inflation than overall inflation is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at core inflation because it’s a better measure of what future inflation is like to be, likely to be, because it’s a better measure of, of what inflation pressures exist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s—it’s complicated, but ultimately, we, you know, our goal is headline, not core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So headline can be affected—you’re talking about next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so headline can, again, it can be affected by energy prices and food prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, there, there will be things in, in the headline forecasts that are to do with forecasts of energy prices, whereas core will be—if, if you look at core going out a full year, then it’ll be much more driven by things like tightness in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it—that, that’s why the two can go in different directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Headline has been lower, as you know, most of this year, but that’s because energy prices have been coming down, which is a great thing for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But energy prices will come down, and then they will go up, and it won’t really be telling us anything about how tight the economy is and how, how future inflation will perform.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we monitor geopolitical risks really quickly, but, you know, but—really carefully, rather.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, I would say so far those risks haven’t really—nothing has come out of those risks that really, has really been important for the United States economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The single thing that you would look to is the price of oil, given that we’re talking about the Middle East and Ukraine, and, you know, and—but that, that is a good summary statistic for the kind of thing that could go wrong in, in, with global turmoil.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the price of oil’s been coming down, and, for, because of supply conditions, global supply conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t—the U.S. is not feeling, really, the effects of geopolitical turmoil, but we are at, certainly, at a time of elevated geopolitical turmoil.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it remains, you know, a risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so inflation—again, we don’t overreact to a couple of months of higher readings or a couple months of lower readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we, what we had was—we had four months of really nice readings, and then September and October were higher, but then November is much lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t really think the public is experiencing that as a surprising upside risk to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think inflation is much lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What the public is feeling, and they’re right about it, is that prices are, are just—the price level went up, because of the past inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is going to take some time to, for real wages to recover, over a period of years in which your, your real compensation is growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, in other words, your compensation’s growing meaningfully faster than inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s exactly the kind of economy we have now, and we just want to hold onto it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that process will probably take some years, but that’s, that’s what’s going on right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t think that, you know, a, a couple of months of higher inflation really signal that, anything of the nature you’re suggesting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re talking about—when you’re projecting the economy, you know, three years out, two years out, you’re talking about high uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very high uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we really—at that point it, it’s not, it’s not possible to confidently predict where the economy is going to be in three years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we’re doing is we’re looking at what’s happening now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re kind of projecting that the same kinds of things are happening—so we, we keep a strong labor market, housing services inflation comes down, goods and services—goods inflation settles down, and, you know, nonmarket services return to their, their prior level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All of those things should happen over time, and, and, you know, those pieces come together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s every reason to think that they will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The timing of it is highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, but you’re not wrong, though, that, you know, we’ve, the— it’s been a bit frustrating because the—while we’ve made progress, it has been slower than we had hoped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, we’re still on track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I think if you’d—if two, two years ago, you’d said, “we were [going to be] at 4.2 percent unemployment and 2.8 percent inflation,” people would be, would say, “I’ll take that.” I mean, that, that’s a pretty good interim place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job’s not done, but, but I think we’re, we’re feeling good about where we are and where we’re headed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, we’re not going to settle for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re, we’re, you know, we certainly have every intention and expectations that we’ll get inflation back sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is—and I am confident we will achieve that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has taken longer, but it’s, you have to be—you know, we are making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have made a great deal of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll continue to do so and get back to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we owe the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, we’re committed to achieving it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t rule things completely in or out in this—in this world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That doesn’t appear to be a likely outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re at 4.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s meaningfully restrictive, and I, I think it’s a well-calibrated rate for us to continue to make progress on inflation while, while keeping a, a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—Thank you very much.
